title: Good Data, Bad Data
desc: Clean and sort data to see how the quality of data shapes what AI learns
content_html:
What We're Doing

In this activity, learners discover why AI systems are only as good as the data they learn from — a concept often summarised as "garbage in, garbage out." Students will work with a messy, realistic dataset (for example, a list of animal descriptions, fruit records, or student survey responses) that contains errors, duplicates, missing values, mislabeled entries, and inconsistent formatting. Working in teams, they will clean and sort this data by hand first, then feed both the "dirty" version and the "cleaned" version into a simple AI classifier or sorting tool to compare results. The goal is for students to directly observe how poor-quality data leads to confused, inaccurate, or biased AI predictions, while clean, well-labeled data leads to confident and correct ones. By the end of the session, learners will understand that data quality — not just clever algorithms — is one of the most important ingredients in building trustworthy AI systems, and they will have practiced real data-cleaning skills: spotting duplicates, fixing typos, standardising formats, handling missing values, and identifying mislabeled data.

Tools & Resources
  • Google Sheets (sheets.google.com) — for viewing, sorting, and cleaning the messy dataset. Free with a Google account.
  • Teachable Machine (teachablemachine.withgoogle.com) — free, browser-based tool to train a simple AI image or text classifier using the "clean" vs "dirty" datasets. No account required; runs entirely in-browser.
  • Prepared dataset handout (provided by facilitator) — a printed or digital spreadsheet of ~30–40 rows of intentionally messy sample data (e.g., animal facts, fruit nutrition data, or weather records) with built-in errors: duplicates, blanks, typos, inconsistent units, and wrong labels.
  • ChatGPT or Gemini (chat.openai.com or gemini.google.com) — optional, for asking the AI to sort/classify the raw messy data vs the cleaned data and compare outputs. Free tiers have daily/usage limits and may occasionally refuse or rate-limit repeated requests — have a backup plan (screenshots of pre-run examples) ready.
  • Pens, sticky notes, or printed cards — for the unplugged sorting warm-up activity.

Step-by-Step Activity

  1. Begin with a 5-minute discussion: ask students "If you taught a friend about animals using a book full of mistakes, what would happen?" Introduce the phrase "garbage in, garbage out."
  2. Hand out the messy dataset (printed cards or shared spreadsheet) containing ~30–40 entries with deliberate issues: duplicate rows, missing fields, inconsistent capitalisation/units, obvious typos, and 3–5 mislabeled entries (e.g., a "cat" labeled as "dog").
  3. In small groups, have students do an unplugged sort first: physically group the cards into categories (e.g., by animal type, fruit type, or weather condition) without fixing anything. Ask them to note what confused them.
  4. Introduce the digital dataset in Google Sheets. Ask groups to identify and highlight at least 5 different types of data problems they can find (duplicates, blanks, typos, wrong labels, inconsistent formats).
  5. Guide students to clean the data: remove duplicates, fill or flag missing values, correct typos, standardise formats (e.g., all lowercase, consistent units), and fix mislabeled rows.
  6. Using Teachable Machine (or ChatGPT/Gemini with a prompt like: "Here is a list of labeled animal descriptions. Sort them into categories based on the label. Note any you're unsure about."), run the ORIGINAL messy dataset through the AI tool and record its classification results/accuracy.
  7. Run the CLEANED dataset through the same AI tool with the same prompt and record the results.
  8. As a class, compare the two result sets side by side: How many errors did the AI make with messy data vs clean data? Did it get confused by duplicates or mislabeled examples?
  9. Each group creates a short "before and after" summary poster or slide showing: one example of a data problem they fixed, and how it changed the AI's output.
  10. Close with a reflection circle: each group shares one surprising thing they learned about how data quality affects AI behaviour.

Example Outputs

Example 1: A group works with an animal dataset where "Elephant" appears as "elephant," "Elefant," and "ELEPHANT, " plus one row mislabeled as "Giraffe." After cleaning, they standardise all spellings and fix the mislabeled row. When run through Teachable Machine, the messy dataset produces 60% classification accuracy with the AI confusing elephants and giraffes; the cleaned dataset produces 95% accuracy with confident, correct groupings.

Example 2: A group working with fruit nutrition data finds 4 duplicate "Banana" rows and 3 rows with missing sugar-content values. They remove duplicates and decide, as a group, to either research correct values or mark missing entries clearly as "unknown" rather than guessing. They create a poster showing "Before: AI said all fruits had similar sugar content" vs "After: AI correctly grouped high-sugar and low-sugar fruits."

Example 3: A group prompts ChatGPT with the messy weather dataset (mixing "Celsius" and "Fahrenheit" without labels) and the AI misclassifies several "hot" days as "cold." After the group standardises all temperatures to Celsius, the AI's classification matches their own human judgement 100% of the time. Their reflection note reads: "The AI wasn't bad at math — our data just didn't make sense."

Facilitation Tips

  • Pre-test the chosen AI tool with your exact dataset before the lesson — Teachable Machine works best with image or short text categories, so keep data simple (short phrases, not paragraphs).
  • Keep the messy dataset genuinely messy but not impossible — 5–7 distinct, clearly identifiable problems are easier to manage than a wall of chaos.
  • Expect the unplugged sorting step to take longer than planned; some groups will want to "fix" the data during sorting — redirect them to first just notice the problems, fixing comes later.
  • If internet access or AI tools are unreliable, have screenshots or printed before/after outputs ready as a backup so the comparison discussion can still happen.
  • Watch for groups who clean too aggressively (deleting rows instead of fixing them) — prompt them to think about what information is lost when you simply delete messy data versus correcting it.
  • Use the mislabeled entries as a teaching moment about bias: ask "What if ALL the mislabeled animals were one type — what might the AI learn wrongly about that animal?"
  • Circulate during the AI comparison step — some groups may be surprised the AI doesn't "notice" errors the way humans do; use this to reinforce that AI does not know right from wrong, it just learns patterns from what it's given.

Discussion Questions

  • What are three specific types of data problems we found in today's messy dataset?
  • Why did the AI perform differently on the messy dataset compared to the cleaned dataset?
  • Can you think of a real-world example where bad data might lead an AI system to make a harmful or unfair decision?
  • If you only had time to fix ONE type of data problem (duplicates, missing values, or wrong labels), which would you prioritise and why?
  • Is it ever okay for an AI to be trained on imperfect data? When might "good enough" data be acceptable, and when is it dangerous?

Extension Challenges

Easy: Take a new, small dataset (10 rows) your facilitator provides and identify all the data problems in under 5 minutes, listing them by type.

Medium: Intentionally introduce 3 new errors into a clean dataset, predict how you think the AI's output will change, then test it and compare your prediction to the actual result.

Hard: Design your own mini "messy dataset" on a topic of your choice (e.g., music genres, sports, local foods), include at least 5 different error types, swap with another group, and have them clean it and test it with an AI tool — then write a short report comparing both groups' before/after accuracy results.
